terms.title: APS-C
terms.subtitle: Crop sensor format, about 1.5× smaller than full frame. Popular in entry-level and semi-pro cameras.
terms.definition: Crop sensor format measuring approximately 23×15 mm, about 1.5× smaller than full frame (35 mm). Popular in entry-level and semi-pro cameras due to lower price and more compact build. The crop factor effectively extends focal length.

terms.title: Autofocus (AF)
terms.subtitle: Automatic focusing of the camera or smartphone. Modern systems detect faces, eyes, animals and objects.
terms.definition: Automatic focusing of the camera or smartphone. Modern systems detect faces, eyes, animals and objects and keep them sharp — essential for movement and fast situations.

terms.title: Resolution
terms.subtitle: The number of pixels in an image. 12 MP = 12 million pixels. Higher resolution means more detail, but not automatically better image quality.
terms.definition: The number of pixels in an image. 12 MP = 12 million pixels. Higher resolution means more detail, but not automatically better image quality. Sensor size and lens quality matter more than megapixels alone.

terms.title: Aperture
terms.subtitle: The lens opening that controls light. Small f-number = large opening = more light and shallow depth of field (bokeh).
terms.definition: The lens opening, measured as f-number (e.g. f/1.8, f/5.6, f/16). Small f-number = large opening = more light and shallow depth of field (strong bokeh). Large f-number = small opening = less light and deep depth of field.

blocks.heading: What does this mean in practice?
blocks.content: The aperture is like the pupil of your eye. In darkness it dilates (small f-number), in brightness it constricts (large f-number). It determines not only brightness but also how much of the image is in focus.

blocks.heading: Real-world example
blocks.content: f/1.8 for portrait: The background becomes softly blurred, the face pops out. f/11 for landscape: Both foreground and horizon are sharp.

terms.title: Backlight
terms.subtitle: Light source behind the subject. Creates silhouettes, lens flare and dramatic mood.
terms.definition: Light source behind the subject shining directly into the lens. Creates silhouettes, lens flare, halo effects and dramatic mood. Popular in portrait and landscape photography for emotionally impactful images.

terms.title: Blue Hour
terms.subtitle: The time shortly before sunrise and after sunset. Cool, bluish light with soft contrast.
terms.definition: The time shortly before sunrise and after sunset, when the sun is 4–8° below the horizon. The light is cooler and bluer than daylight, with soft contrast and dramatic skies. Ideal for cityscapes and landscapes.

terms.title: Bokeh
terms.subtitle: The aesthetic quality of background blur. Good bokeh is soft and creamy, bad bokeh looks busy.
terms.definition: The aesthetic quality of background blur. Created by large aperture opening (small f-number) and shallow depth of field. Good bokeh is soft and creamy, bad bokeh looks busy or double-edged.

terms.title: Brightness
terms.subtitle: The perceived light intensity of an image. Fundamental property of exposure.
terms.definition: The perceived light intensity of an image or image area. Determined by exposure, aperture and shutter speed. In post-processing, brightness can be adjusted locally or globally without destroying contrast relationships.

terms.title: Exposure
terms.subtitle: The amount of light hitting the sensor. Controlled by aperture, shutter speed and ISO.
terms.definition: The amount of light that hits the sensor and makes the image bright or dark. Controlled by the exposure triangle: aperture (light amount), shutter speed (duration) and ISO (sensitivity).

terms.title: Exposure Triangle
terms.subtitle: The three parameters that control exposure: aperture, shutter speed and ISO. Change one, and you must adjust at least one other.
terms.definition: The three parameters that control exposure: aperture, shutter speed and ISO. Change one, and you must adjust at least one other to maintain the same brightness. Understanding this triangle is the foundation of photography.

blocks.heading: What does this mean in practice?
blocks.content: The exposure triangle is the foundation of photography. Aperture controls light amount and depth of field, shutter speed controls motion, and ISO controls the sensor's light sensitivity. Every combination yields a specific exposure.

blocks.heading: The Analogy
blocks.content: Imagine a window: The aperture is the window size, the shutter speed is how long the curtain stays open, and ISO is the sensitivity of your eyes. All three determine how much light comes in.

terms.title: Focal Length
terms.subtitle: Determines the angle of view and perspective. Short focal lengths (wide angle) show a lot, long focal lengths (telephoto) zoom in.
terms.definition: Determines the angle of view and perspective. Short focal lengths (wide angle, e.g. 18mm) show lots of environment and emphasize depth. Long focal lengths (telephoto, e.g. 200mm) zoom in and compress space.

terms.title: Image Editing
terms.subtitle: Digital post-processing of photos. Includes development, retouching, color correction and export.
terms.definition: The digital post-processing of photos after capture. Includes RAW development, exposure correction, color adjustment, retouching, cropping and exporting to various file formats. Tools: GIMP, darktable, Lightroom.

terms.title: Image Noise
terms.subtitle: Digital grain, especially at high ISO values or with small sensors. Appears as colorful or monochrome speckles.
terms.definition: Digital grain in images, especially at high ISO values or with small sensors. Appears as colorful or monochrome speckles. Can be mitigated through noise reduction in post-processing.

terms.title: Image Stabilization (IBIS / OIS)
terms.subtitle: Compensates for camera shake for sharper images at longer shutter speeds.
terms.definition: Compensates for camera shake through moving sensor elements (In-Body) or moving lens groups (Optical). Enables sharper images at longer shutter speeds without a tripod. Modern systems achieve 5–8 stops of compensation.

terms.title: Chromatic Aberration
terms.subtitle: Color fringing at high-contrast edges, usually visible as red or green borders. Especially common in cheap lenses.
terms.definition: Color fringing at high-contrast edges, usually visible as red or green borders. Especially common in cheap lenses or at maximum aperture opening. Can be corrected in post-processing.

terms.title: Color Grading
terms.subtitle: Creative color design of an image. Creates mood, look and recognizability.
terms.definition: The creative color design of an image using color curves, color wheels and selective adjustments. Unlike correction (fixing errors), this is about mood, look and recognizability. The foundation of a personal photography style.

terms.title: Computational Photography
terms.subtitle: Software-powered photography. Smartphones use AI and algorithms to compensate for physical sensor limitations.
terms.definition: Software-powered photography. Smartphones use AI and algorithms (HDR, Portrait mode, Night mode) to compensate for physical sensor limitations and improve image quality beyond what the hardware alone can achieve.

terms.title: Contrast
terms.subtitle: The difference between bright and dark areas. Determines image impact and drama.
terms.definition: The difference between bright and dark areas in an image. High contrast looks dramatic and bold, low contrast looks soft and dreamy. Influenced by exposure, light quality and post-processing.

terms.title: Cropping
terms.subtitle: Removing image edges to improve composition. Changes aspect ratio and framing.
terms.definition: Removing image edges to improve composition. Changes the aspect ratio, strengthens the main subject and can correct composition afterward. Non-destructive in RAW programs.

terms.title: Curves
terms.subtitle: Tool for precise tonal correction. Controls brightness and contrast point by point.
terms.definition: A tool for precise tonal correction in post-processing. Curves allow brightness and contrast to be controlled point by point for every tonal range — more powerful than simple sliders.

terms.title: Distortion
terms.subtitle: Lens aberration that makes straight lines appear curved. Wide angles tend toward barrel or pincushion distortion.
terms.definition: A lens aberration that makes straight lines appear curved. Wide angles tend toward barrel distortion (lines bend outward), telephotos toward pincushion distortion (lines bend inward). Can be corrected in post-processing.

terms.title: DNG / Smartphone RAW
terms.subtitle: RAW format for smartphones. Stores uncompressed sensor data for maximum editing flexibility.
terms.definition: RAW format for smartphones (Digital Negative). Stores uncompressed sensor data for maximum editing flexibility — available in many camera apps in Pro mode. Larger files than JPEG, but significantly more editing headroom.

terms.title: Dynamic Range
terms.subtitle: The brightness range a sensor can capture simultaneously. Larger sensors typically have higher dynamic range.
terms.definition: The brightness range a sensor can capture simultaneously — from the darkest shadows to the brightest highlights. Larger sensors typically have higher dynamic range than smartphone sensors.

terms.title: Rule of Thirds
terms.subtitle: Divide the image mentally into nine equal parts (3×3). Place the main subject at an intersection or along a line.
terms.definition: Divide the image mentally into nine equal parts (3×3). Place the main subject at an intersection or along a line. Looks more natural than central placement and creates tension in the image.

blocks.heading: What does this mean in practice?
blocks.content: The rule of thirds is the most well-known composition rule. It uses the natural reading behavior of the eye, which wanders to the intersection points of the 3×3 grid rather than the center.

blocks.heading: Why is this important?
blocks.content: Central placements often appear static and boring. The rule of thirds creates dynamism and deliberately guides the viewer's eye through the image.

terms.title: EXIF / Metadata
terms.subtitle: Hidden information in every photo: camera, lens, exposure, GPS coordinates, timestamp.
terms.definition: Hidden information in every photo: camera used, lens, aperture, shutter speed, ISO, GPS coordinates, timestamp. Useful for analyzing your own photos, but also a privacy risk when sharing.

terms.title: Color Temperature
terms.subtitle: Measured in Kelvin (K). Daylight ≈ 5500K, tungsten ≈ 2700K, shade ≈ 7000K. Determines the color tone of light.
terms.definition: Measured in Kelvin (K). Daylight ≈ 5500K, tungsten ≈ 2700K (warm/yellow), shade ≈ 7000K (cold/blue). Determines the color tone of light and must be corrected via white balance.

terms.title: Flash / Speedlight
terms.subtitle: Short artificial light to brighten scenes. Enables photos in low light and freezes motion.
terms.definition: Short-duration artificial light (approx. 1/1000s or faster) to brighten scenes. Enables photos in low light, freezes motion and can be used for creative effects. Speedlights are portable, studio strobes offer more power.

terms.title: Focus Stacking
terms.subtitle: Multiple images with different focus points are combined into one image. Ideal for macro and product photography.
terms.definition: Multiple images with different focus points are combined into a single image that is sharp everywhere. Ideal for macro and product photography where depth of field in a single image is insufficient.

terms.title: Framing
terms.subtitle: Using natural elements around the subject as a picture frame. Focuses attention.
terms.definition: Using natural elements in the foreground (branches, doors, windows, caves) around the subject as a picture frame. Focuses the viewer's attention on the main subject and creates depth through layers.

terms.title: Full Frame
terms.subtitle: 35 mm film-sized sensor (36×24 mm). Best image quality, highest dynamic range.
terms.definition: A sensor the size of a classic 35 mm film (36×24 mm). Offers the best image quality, highest dynamic range and lowest noise. The reference standard for professional photography, but more expensive and heavier.

terms.title: Leading Lines
terms.subtitle: Lines in the image that guide the viewer's eye to the main subject. Roads, fences, shorelines.
terms.definition: Natural or artificial lines in the image that deliberately guide the viewer's eye to the main subject. Roads, fences, shorelines, architectural lines or shadows can act as leading lines. Creates depth and dynamism.

terms.title: Prime Lens
terms.subtitle: Fixed focal length lens. Usually faster, sharper and more compact than zooms.
terms.definition: Lens with a fixed focal length (e.g. 35 mm, 50 mm, 85 mm). Usually faster (small f-number), sharper and more compact than zoom lenses. Forces more conscious composition since the photographer must "zoom with their feet".

terms.title: Golden Hour
terms.subtitle: The hour shortly after sunrise and before sunset. Warm, soft light with long shadows — the best light for almost everything.
terms.definition: The hour shortly after sunrise and before sunset. Warm, soft light with long shadows — the best light for almost all genres. Color temperature is approximately 3000–3500K.

blocks.heading: Real-world example
blocks.content: Portrait at Golden Hour: The warm light makes skin tones look soft and healthy. Landscape at Golden Hour: Long shadows create depth and drama.

terms.title: ND Filter (Neutral Density)
terms.subtitle: Dark glass in front of the lens that reduces light. Enables long shutter speeds in daylight.
terms.definition: Dark glass in front of the lens that reduces light without distorting colors. Enables long shutter speeds in daylight (silky water effect) or wide apertures in sunshine.

terms.title: HDR
terms.subtitle: High Dynamic Range. Combines multiple exposures into one image with higher dynamic range.
terms.definition: High Dynamic Range. Combines multiple exposures into one image with higher dynamic range. Rescues details in highlights and shadows — especially important on smartphones with small sensors.

terms.title: High Key
terms.subtitle: Bright, airy image style with few shadows. Radiates joy and lightness.
terms.definition: A bright, airy image style with predominantly light tones and few shadows. Radiates joy, lightness and elegance. Popular in portrait, product and fashion photography. Requires lots of light or deliberate overexposure.

terms.title: Histogram
terms.subtitle: Graphical representation of brightness distribution in an image. Ideal for recognizing over- and underexposure.
terms.definition: Graphical representation of brightness distribution in an image. The X-axis shows brightness (black on the left, white on the right), the Y-axis shows how many pixels have that brightness. Ideal for recognizing over- and underexposure.

blocks.heading: What does this mean in practice?
blocks.content: If the graph is clipped at the left edge, shadows are underexposed (lost details). If clipped at the right edge, highlights are overexposed (blown out). A balanced histogram stretches from left to right without clipping.

terms.title: ISO
terms.subtitle: Sensor light sensitivity. Higher values enable photos in low light but create more noise.
terms.definition: Sensor light sensitivity. Higher values (e.g. ISO 3200) enable photos in low light but create more image noise. Lower values (e.g. ISO 100) deliver cleaner images in good light.

blocks.heading: What does this mean in practice?
blocks.content: ISO is your emergency dial. When you don't have enough light and can't open the aperture further or lengthen the shutter speed, you increase the ISO. Modern cameras work cleanly at ISO 3200, while smartphones show noise already at ISO 800.

blocks.heading: Real-world example
blocks.content: ISO 100 in bright sunshine: Crystal clear images without noise. ISO 1600 by candlelight: The image is bright enough but shows grain.

terms.title: JPEG
terms.subtitle: Standard image format with lossy compression. Small files but limited editing headroom.
terms.definition: The standard image format with lossy compression. Produces small files that can be shared directly. Disadvantage: Limited editing headroom since brightness, color and white balance are permanently embedded.

terms.title: Composition
terms.subtitle: The arrangement of elements in the image. Determines how the viewer's eye is guided.
terms.definition: The arrangement of elements in the image. Determines how the viewer's eye is guided and what emotions the image evokes. The most well-known rule is the rule of thirds.

terms.title: Lens
terms.subtitle: The eye of the camera. Determines focal length, speed, sharpness and image quality.
terms.definition: The eye of the camera. Determines focal length (angle of view), speed (f-number), sharpness, bokeh and image quality. A more important investment than the camera body, as good lenses last for decades.

terms.title: Lens Flare
terms.subtitle: Light reflections in the lens that appear as circles, streaks or glow in the image. Can be artistic or distracting.
terms.definition: Light reflections in the lens that appear as circles, streaks or glow in the image. Occurs with backlighting. Can be used artistically or considered a flaw — depending on the desired effect.

terms.title: Long Exposure
terms.subtitle: Shutter speeds of several seconds to minutes. Transforms water into silk and clouds into streaks.
terms.definition: Shutter speeds of several seconds to minutes. Transforms moving water into silk, clouds into streaks, and creates light trails. Requires a tripod and often an ND filter in daylight.

terms.title: Low Key
terms.subtitle: Dark, dramatic image style with many shadows. Creates tension and intimacy.
terms.definition: A dark, dramatic image style with predominantly dark tones and targeted light accents. Creates tension, intimacy and three-dimensionality. Popular in portrait and film-noir photography. Requires targeted lighting setup.

terms.title: Macro
terms.subtitle: Photography of very small subjects at a 1:1 magnification ratio or greater. Reveals details invisible to the naked eye.
terms.definition: Photography of very small subjects at a 1:1 magnification ratio or greater. A 1cm subject is reproduced 1cm or larger on the sensor. Reveals details invisible to the naked eye.

terms.title: Monochrome / Black & White
terms.subtitle: Images in a single color tone. Removes distraction and emphasizes form, structure and contrast.
terms.definition: Images in a single color tone — classically black and white (grayscale), but also sepia, cyanotype or any other single color. Removes color distraction and emphasizes form, structure, texture and contrast.

terms.title: Moodboard
terms.subtitle: Visual collection of ideas, colors and moods. Serves as creative guideline for a photo project.
terms.definition: A visual collection of images, colors, textures and moods that serves as a creative guideline for a photo project. Helps define look, style and atmosphere before the shoot and align the team.

terms.title: Natural Light
terms.subtitle: Sunlight in all variations: Harsh midday light, soft overcast light, warm evening light.
terms.definition: Sunlight in all variations — from harsh midday light to soft overcast light to warm evening light. Costs nothing, is available everywhere and can be controlled with reflectors and diffusers. The foundation of most photography.

terms.title: Negative Space
terms.subtitle: The empty area around a subject. Emphasizes the subject and lets the image breathe.
terms.definition: The empty area around a subject. Emphasizes the subject, lets the image breathe, and creates calm. Minimalism can be very powerful — not every image needs to be full.

terms.title: Night Mode
terms.subtitle: Smartphone feature for dark scenes. Combines multiple exposures through image stabilization into one bright, low-noise image.
terms.definition: Smartphone feature for dark scenes. Combines multiple exposures through image stabilization into one bright, low-noise image. Requires a steady phone or tripod for best results.

terms.title: Noise Reduction
terms.subtitle: Filter that reduces digital grain. Must be used carefully to preserve detail.
terms.definition: A filter in post-processing that reduces digital grain (image noise). Must be used carefully, as too much noise reduction blurs details. Modern AI tools work significantly better here than classic algorithms.

terms.title: Panorama
terms.subtitle: Wide-format image composed of multiple individual shots. Ideal for wide-angle scenes.
terms.definition: Wide-format image composed of multiple individual shots. Smartphones usually offer an automatic panorama mode. Movement during capture can cause distortions.

terms.title: Perspective
terms.subtitle: Spatial representation of depth in the image. Influenced by camera position and focal length.
terms.definition: The spatial representation of depth and three-dimensionality in a two-dimensional image. Influenced by camera position (height, angle, distance) and focal length. Wide angle emphasizes depth, telephoto compresses space.

terms.title: PNG
terms.subtitle: Lossless image format with transparency support. Ideal for graphics and screenshots.
terms.definition: Lossless image format with transparency support (alpha channel). Ideal for graphics, logos, screenshots and images with sharp edges. Larger files than JPEG but without quality loss.

terms.title: Portrait Mode
terms.subtitle: Smartphone mode that simulates background blur via software. Uses depth maps from multiple cameras or AI.
terms.definition: Smartphone mode that simulates background blur (bokeh) via software. Uses depth maps from multiple cameras or AI-based object detection. Works well with clear contours but can create artifacts with hair or fine details.

terms.title: Preset
terms.subtitle: Saved editing settings for repeatable looks. Saves time and ensures consistency.
terms.definition: Saved editing settings (e.g. for exposure, color, contrast, sharpness) that can be applied to any image with one click. Saves time and ensures consistent look across entire series.

terms.title: Pro Mode (Smartphone)
terms.subtitle: Manual camera mode on smartphones. Allows setting shutter speed, ISO, white balance and focus.
terms.definition: Manual camera mode on smartphones. Allows setting shutter speed, ISO, white balance and focus — just like on a dedicated camera. Available in most stock camera apps and professional apps like Lightroom Mobile.

terms.title: Noise / Image Noise
terms.subtitle: Digital grain in images, especially at high ISO values or with small sensors. Appears as colorful or monochrome speckles.
terms.definition: Digital grain in images, especially at high ISO values or with small sensors (smartphones). Appears as colorful or monochrome speckles. Can be mitigated through noise reduction in post-processing.

terms.title: RAW
terms.subtitle: Uncompressed image format with maximum editing potential. Stores all sensor data without quality loss.
terms.definition: Uncompressed image format with maximum editing potential. Stores all sensor data without quality loss. Allows post-capture correction of exposure, white balance and more. Files are significantly larger than JPEG.

blocks.heading: What does this mean in practice?
blocks.content: JPEG is like a finished dish — you can only add salt and pepper. RAW is like all ingredients separate — you can change the recipe afterward.

blocks.heading: Why is this important?
blocks.content: RAW gives you maximum flexibility in post-processing. You can rescue overexposure, correct white balance, and use more dynamic range. Essential for serious photography.

terms.title: RAW Development
terms.subtitle: Converting RAW sensor data into a visible image. First step in a professional workflow.
terms.definition: The conversion of RAW sensor data into a visible image. First step in a professional workflow: white balance, exposure, contrast, sharpness and color are set. Tools: darktable, Lightroom, RawTherapee.

terms.title: Reflector
terms.subtitle: Surface that bounces light back. Used to brighten shadows and control light.
terms.definition: A surface (gold, silver, white, black, translucent) that bounces light back or absorbs it. Used to brighten shadows, create catchlights or soften harsh light. An inexpensive and versatile lighting tool.

terms.title: Reportage / Documentary
terms.subtitle: Authentic representation of events and stories. No staging, just observation.
terms.definition: Authentic representation of events, people and stories through photography. No staging, just observation and documentation of real life. Requires speed, empathy and technical confidence.

terms.title: Depth of Field
terms.subtitle: Area in front of and behind the focus point that appears sharp. Influenced by aperture, focal length and focus distance.
terms.definition: Area in front of and behind the focus point that appears sharp. Influenced by aperture (small f-number = shallow), focal length (longer = shallower) and focus distance (closer = shallower).

blocks.heading: What does this mean in practice?
blocks.content: At f/1.8 and 85mm, only the model's eye is sharp — everything else blurs softly (bokeh). At f/11 and 24mm, both foreground and horizon are sharp.

terms.title: Saturation
terms.subtitle: The intensity of colors in an image. High saturation looks vivid, low looks soft.
terms.definition: The intensity or purity of colors in an image. High saturation looks vivid and eye-catching, low saturation looks soft, nostalgic or dramatic (with monochrome). An important parameter in post-processing.

terms.title: Sensor
terms.subtitle: The digital equivalent of film. Converts light into electrical signals. Size determines image quality.
terms.definition: The digital equivalent of film in a camera. Converts incoming light into electrical signals. Sensor size largely determines image quality, dynamic range and noise behavior. Bigger is almost always better.

terms.title: Sharpness
terms.subtitle: Clarity of contours and details. Determined by focus, aperture and lens quality.
terms.definition: The clarity of contours and details in an image. Determined by correct focus, aperture choice, lens quality and camera stability. Too much sharpening looks artificial. Sharpness is not an end in itself but a creative tool.

terms.title: Silhouette
terms.subtitle: Dark shape against a bright background. Created by strong backlight where the subject is underexposed.
terms.definition: Dark shape against a bright background. Created by strong backlight where the subject is underexposed. On smartphone: Tap the bright sky to render the subject as a silhouette.

terms.title: Softbox
terms.subtitle: Light modifier with diffusing front panel. Creates soft, even light with gentle shadows.
terms.definition: A light modifier with a diffusing front panel that transforms harsh flash light into soft, even light. Creates gentle shadows and is ideal for portrait and product photography. Available in many sizes from 30 cm to 2 m.

terms.title: Storytelling
terms.subtitle: Telling stories through images. More than technique — it's about emotion and message.
terms.definition: Telling stories, emotions and messages through single images or image series. More than technique: it's about captivating the viewer, asking questions and enabling an emotional journey.

terms.title: Symmetry
terms.subtitle: Balance in an image through mirroring or repetition. Appears harmonious and calm.
terms.definition: Balance in an image through mirroring, repetition or even distribution of elements. Appears harmonious, calm and aesthetically satisfying. Popular in architecture, nature and product photography.

terms.title: Telephoto Lens
terms.subtitle: Long focal length (from 70 mm). Zooms in, compresses space and isolates the subject.
terms.definition: A lens with long focal length (from 70 mm, typically 70–200 mm or 100–400 mm). Zooms in, compresses space, isolates the subject from the background and creates flat perspective. Ideal for portrait, sports, wildlife and details.

terms.title: Texture
terms.subtitle: Surface structure visible in the image. Side light emphasizes texture especially strongly.
terms.definition: The visible surface structure of materials in an image — wood, stone, skin, fabric, metal. Emphasized by light quality: side light shows texture most strongly, front light washes it out. An important design tool.

terms.title: TIFF
terms.subtitle: Lossless archive format with high bit depth. Ideal for print and professional workflows.
terms.definition: A lossless archive format with high bit depth (16 bit per channel). Supports layers, transparency and various color spaces. Ideal for print, professional workflows and as an intermediate step between RAW and JPEG.

terms.title: Tonal Value
terms.subtitle: The brightness of a single pixel. From black (0) through gray to white (255).
terms.definition: The brightness of a single pixel or area in the image. In 8-bit images from 0 (pure black) to 255 (pure white). Tonal values determine contrast, brightness and the effect of light and shadow.

terms.title: Tripod
terms.subtitle: Three-legged stand for the camera. Essential for long exposures, macro and sharp images.
terms.definition: A three-legged stand that stabilizes the camera. Essential for long exposures, macro, astrophotography, panoramas and sharp images in low light. Available in aluminum or carbon fiber, with ball or pan heads.

terms.title: Shutter Speed
terms.subtitle: Duration the sensor receives light. Short speeds freeze motion, long speeds create motion blur.
terms.definition: Duration the sensor receives light. Short speeds (e.g. 1/1000s) freeze motion. Long speeds (e.g. 1/30s or several seconds) create motion blur or light trails. Affects brightness and motion.

blocks.heading: Real-world example
blocks.content: 1/1000s: A jumping dog is frozen sharp. 1/60s: The dog has slight motion blur — looks dynamic. 2s: The dog is only a blurred shadow.

terms.title: Vignetting
terms.subtitle: Darkening at the image edges. Can occur naturally through the lens or be added artistically.
terms.definition: Darkening at the image edges. Can occur naturally through the lens (especially at wide apertures) or be added artistically in post-processing. Draws the eye toward the image center.

terms.title: WebP
terms.subtitle: Modern Google format for the web. Offers better compression than JPEG at equal quality.
terms.definition: A modern image format from Google for web applications. Offers significantly smaller files than JPEG at equal quality and also supports transparency and animation. Supported by all modern browsers.

terms.title: White Balance (WB)
terms.subtitle: Color temperature correction for neutral colors. Adjusts the camera for different light sources.
terms.definition: Color temperature correction for neutral colors. Adjusts the camera for different light sources: Daylight (5200K), Cloudy (6000K), Tungsten (3200K), Fluorescent (4000K). Correctable after capture with RAW files.

blocks.heading: What does this mean in practice?
blocks.content: Without white balance, a photo under tungsten light looks too yellow and in shade too blue. White balance tells the camera what 'white' is so all other colors are rendered correctly.

terms.title: Wide Angle
terms.subtitle: Short focal length (up to 35 mm). Shows lots of environment, emphasizes depth and perspective.
terms.definition: A lens with short focal length (up to 35 mm). Shows lots of environment, emphasizes depth and perspective, magnifies close areas and minimizes distant areas. Ideal for landscape, architecture, astro and street photography.

terms.title: Zoom: Digital vs. Optical
terms.subtitle: Optical zoom magnifies through lenses — no quality loss. Digital zoom only enlarges pixels — quality suffers.
terms.definition: Optical zoom magnifies through moving lenses — no quality loss. Digital zoom only enlarges pixels (cropping) — image quality suffers. On smartphones, better use the fixed optical cameras instead of zooming.
